title: Who do you say I am? (Matthew 16:13–20)
hookLine: Peter answers first, and is given a name meaning rock and the keys of the kingdom

lines: WHO DO YOU THINK THEY ARE?
AN EASY QUESTION, THEN A HARD ONE.
cards: People ask what you do for work, where you're from, what you're into. It's rare that someone asks who you think they are.
Matthew sets this scene in the far north, in the region of Caesarea Philippi, a town whose very name honored Caesar.
Jesus and his disciples are walking, and he asks an easy question first: what are people saying about me? Then a hard one.

teach.h: WHOM DO MEN SAY THAT I AM?
teach.b: The easy one, in the King James Bible: "Whom do men say that I the Son of man am?" Some say John the Baptist, back from the dead. Some say Elijah.
Others, Jeremiah, or one of the prophets.
Then he turns it: "But whom say ye that I am?" You, not the crowds. Peter answers: "Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God."
Christ is the Greek for the Hebrew Messiah: the anointed one, the king God promised. Jesus calls him blessed, and says this came not from any human being but from his Father in heaven.
Then he gives Simon a new name: "thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it." There's a pun inside.
In Greek, Peter is Petros, and rock is petra. John's Gospel gives Peter's name in Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke, as Cephas, which it says means a stone; Paul calls him Cephas too.
Some readers hear one Aramaic word, kepha, under both halves of the line. Then: "And I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven."

teach.h: THE KEYS: WHO OPENS AND SHUTS.
teach.b: Keys meant authority, the steward of a house who opens and shuts the doors. Here Christians read differently, and deeply.
Catholics understand the rock as Peter himself, his authority passed on to the bishops of Rome; the keys appear on the papal coat of arms.
Orthodox Christians honor Peter as first among the apostles, and many of their teachers read the rock as Peter's confession of faith, with authority held by the bishops together.
Many Protestants read the rock as that confession, or as Christ himself. The question reads the same in every Bible: who do you say I am?

how: Catholics keep the Chair of Saint Peter on February 22, and churches East and West keep Saints Peter and Paul on June 29. Many Christians describe coming to faith as answering this question for themselves, and some churches ask it in confirmation or at baptism.

games.q: you're one of the disciples. Jesus has asked what people say about him, and you've answered. now he asks: but who do you say I am? what do you do?
o: say: thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God.
stay quiet and wait for someone else.
games.why: Peter answers first, and Jesus calls him blessed, gives him a name meaning rock, and promises him the keys.

practice: Let the question come to you as it came to them: not what your parents, church, friends or the internet say, but who do you say he is?
A teacher, a prophet, the Christ, a question mark, someone you're still meeting; nobody's grading, so be honest. If you pray, you can bring your answer to God as it is.

wordCard.voice: The keys. The authority to open and shut, given to Peter, the rock, after he answered the hard question. Churches read the keys in different ways.

orig.note: Greek: Peter, a stone. Beside petra, a rock, it makes the pun at the heart of this story.

carryVoice: Your line: the question is for you. Six days later, three friends climb a mountain. Day fifty-seven counts.
